title: Tukaram's Sugarcane
hookLine: a saint gives away his sugarcane, and his wife breaks the last stalk on his back
carry: it's all the Lord's, even the last stalk
tomorrow: What would you do if you were told to drown your songs?

cards: A man walks home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. You peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up.
Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then the next, and the next.
By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, with a household to feed. The man is Tukaram.

teach.b: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river, a devotee of Vitthal, the same god Namdev sang to.
Tradition says Namdev came to him in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs.
Tradition says his shop failed and famine took people he loved, and out of that grief he turned his whole life toward Vitthal.
Back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is furious. The story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away.

She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me.

teach.h: ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.
teach.b: It's funny. It's also an old Hindu teaching, lived with a stick of cane.

The Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this, everything that moves in the world, is dwelt in by the Lord. So enjoy it by letting go, and don't grasp: whose is the wealth, anyway? Nothing Tukaram holds is his.
It's Vitthal's, passing through his hands, to the children, and then to the wife who's angry with him. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane.
His Varkari tradition holds up exactly this: a householder with debts and a hungry family, singing to Vitthal in the middle of it.

how: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.

o: a hermit who left his family to live in a cave
the grocer-saint of Dehu who gave the sugarcane away
the learned man who said a grocer shouldn't sing

p: came to him in a dream
snapped in two across his back

s: Tukaram was a hermit who left home for the forest
he's remembered as a grocer and a husband in the village of Dehu.
the Isha Upanishad says all this belongs to the Lord, so don't grasp
enjoy it by letting go, it says: whose is the wealth?
Tukaram shouted back when the stalk broke

games.q: you're Tukaram, walking home with an armful of sugarcane. children run up and ask for some. what do you do?
o: keep it all; your family needs it.
give one to each child who asks.
sell it to them for a coin each.
games.why: he hands it out stalk by stalk and gets home with one. when it breaks across his back, he splits it with his wife.

practice: Before you eat today, pause over the plate, the way many Hindu families offer food to God before a meal and then eat it as prasad, a gift given back. Say inwardly, this is yours, Lord, or simply, this isn't only mine.
Then think of one thing you've been gripping, and ask Tukaram's question: whose is it, really? If you don't pray, hold the plate a moment in thanks.

wordCard.voice: Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.

orig.note: Marathi, in Devanagari: the saint's name.

carryVoice: Your line: it's all the Lord's, even the last stalk. Tukaram held nothing as his own, so even a broken stalk got shared. Until tomorrow.
